blocks.text: A 32-year-old man who injects drugs has had three weeks of fevers and night sweats, a new pansystolic murmur at the left lower sternal edge and pleuritic chest pain with multiple round shadows on his chest X-ray. Blood taken before the first antibiotic dose will decide the diagnosis. Infective endocarditis is easy to miss and fatal if missed, and a different group of conditions, the cardiomyopathies, can fail the heart's muscle without any valve infection at all.

blocks.markdown:
**Mechanism of infective endocarditis (IE).** Damaged endothelium (from turbulent flow over a valve lesion, a prosthesis, or direct injury such as injecting drugs) exposes collagen, and platelets and fibrin deposit as a sterile thrombus. Bacteraemia then seeds this thrombus and the organisms multiply behind a fibrin shield, forming a **vegetation** that is poorly accessible to host defences. Consequences are local (valve destruction causing regurgitation, abscess, new conduction block), embolic (stroke, splenic or renal infarcts, septic pulmonary emboli with right-sided disease) and immunological (immune-complex deposition causing glomerulonephritis, Osler nodes and Roth spots).

Typical organisms: *viridans streptococci* (subacute, native valve with prior damage), *Staphylococcus aureus* (acute, aggressive, drug use and healthcare-related), *enterococci*, coagulase-negative staphylococci (prosthetic valves) and the HACEK group (slow-growing Gram-negative organisms).

blocks.caption: Modified Duke criteria (summary). Definite IE: 2 major, or 1 major plus 3 minor, or 5 minor criteria.
rows: Typical organism in two separate blood-culture sets (viridans streptococci, Streptococcus gallolyticus, HACEK, Staphylococcus aureus, community-acquired enterococci), or persistently positive cultures
Echocardiographic vegetation, abscess or new partial dehiscence of a prosthetic valve, or new valvular regurgitation
Prior IE, prosthetic valve, valve disease, congenital heart disease, injecting drug use
Temperature at or above 38.0 degrees Celsius
Major arterial emboli, septic pulmonary infarcts, mycotic aneurysm, intracranial haemorrhage, Janeway lesions, conjunctival haemorrhages
Glomerulonephritis, Osler nodes, Roth spots, positive rheumatoid factor
Positive blood culture not meeting a major criterion

blocks.title: Blood culture strategy
blocks.text: Take at least three sets of blood cultures (each a separate venepuncture site, aerobic and anaerobic bottles) before starting antibiotics, spaced over at least an hour when the patient is stable. In a very unwell patient, take them quickly and treat without delay. Multiple positive sets with the same organism show a continuous bacteraemia. Culture-negative endocarditis is usually due to prior antibiotic exposure or fastidious organisms (HACEK, Coxiella, Bartonella). Transthoracic echocardiography is the first imaging test; transoesophageal echocardiography is more sensitive, especially for prosthetic valves and abscesses.

blocks.title: Applying the Duke criteria
blocks.prompt: A 61-year-old man with a bioprosthetic aortic valve has a temperature of 38.9 degrees Celsius and Osler nodes on his fingers. Two separate blood-culture sets grow Staphylococcus aureus. Echocardiography is awaited. How is the case classified at this stage?

steps.text: Major criterion: Staphylococcus aureus in two separate sets (typical organism). Count 1 major.
Minor criteria: predisposition (prosthetic valve), fever at or above 38.0 degrees Celsius, and an immunological phenomenon (Osler nodes). Count 3 minor.
1 major plus 3 minor meets the definition of definite endocarditis, even before the echocardiogram.

blocks.answer: Definite infective endocarditis; start treatment, with echocardiography to assess complications.

blocks.markdown:
**Cardiomyopathy** means disease of the myocardium itself, not caused by valve, coronary, hypertensive or congenital disease. The main phenotypes are:

- **Dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM):** dilated, thin-walled ventricles with reduced systolic function. Causes include genetic variants, alcohol, viral myocarditis, peripartum, chemotherapy (anthracyclines) and persistent tachycardia. Presents as heart failure and arrhythmia.
- **Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM):** unexplained left ventricular hypertrophy (commonly wall thickness 15 mm or more), often asymmetric septal; autosomal dominant sarcomere gene mutations. May obstruct the left ventricular outflow tract (LVOT). Presents with exertional dyspnoea, chest pain, syncope, palpitations or sudden cardiac death in young people.
- **Restrictive cardiomyopathy:** stiff, non-compliant ventricles with impaired filling and often preserved ejection fraction; causes include amyloidosis and sarcoidosis. Presents with right-sided signs such as a raised JVP (with Kussmaul sign, a paradoxical rise in venous pressure on inspiration) and oedema.
- **Others:** arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy and stress (Takotsubo) cardiomyopathy.

blocks.caption: Cardiomyopathy comparison.
rows: Displaced apex, third heart sound, global hypokinesia on echocardiogram
Thick LV (often septum), hyperdynamic, outflow obstruction
Ejection systolic murmur louder on standing or Valsalva and softer on squatting
Stiff walls, impaired filling, preserved EF
Raised JVP with Kussmaul sign, low-voltage ECG with thick walls in amyloid
T-wave inversion V1 to V3, epsilon waves

blocks.caption: Left ventricular ejection fraction from end-diastolic volume (EDV) and end-systolic volume (ESV).

blocks.title: Ejection fraction and the left ventricular outflow gradient
blocks.prompt: On echocardiography, a patient has EDV 150 mL and ESV 60 mL. Separately, in another patient with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, continuous-wave Doppler across the LVOT shows a peak velocity of 3.0 m/s. Calculate the ejection fraction in the first patient and the peak LVOT pressure gradient in the second, using the simplified Bernoulli equation.

steps.text: Stroke volume = EDV - ESV = 150 - 60 = 90 mL, so ejection fraction = 90 / 150 x 100 = 60%, which is normal.
The simplified Bernoulli equation gives pressure gradient = 4 x v squared, with v in metres per second and the result in mmHg.
For v = 3.0 m/s: 4 x 3.0 squared = 4 x 9 = 36 mmHg. A resting gradient of 30 mmHg or more indicates LVOT obstruction in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.

blocks.answer: Ejection fraction 60% (normal); LVOT gradient 36 mmHg (obstruction present).

blocks.markdown: **Antibiotic prophylaxis (o3).** Bacteraemia from dental procedures was once believed to be the main cause of endocarditis, so prophylaxis before dental work was widely prescribed. The principle now is that prophylaxis prevents very few cases (everyday activities such as chewing and tooth brushing cause far more cumulative bacteraemia than a single procedure), antibiotics themselves cause adverse reactions, and good oral hygiene matters more. **UK guidance does not recommend routine antibiotic prophylaxis** against endocarditis for dental or other procedures, even in patients at higher risk, and stresses oral hygiene, regular dental review and early treatment of infection. Some other international guidelines (for example European) still restrict prophylaxis to the **highest-risk** group (prosthetic valves, previous endocarditis, certain congenital heart disease) undergoing high-risk dental procedures. Patients should know the symptoms of IE and seek early review for unexplained fever.

items: Treat IE with prolonged intravenous bactericidal antibiotics chosen by organism and sensitivities, guided by a multidisciplinary endocarditis team.
Indications for early surgery include heart failure from valve destruction, uncontrolled infection or abscess, and recurrent emboli despite therapy.
Source control: remove or treat the portal of entry, such as dental sepsis or infected lines.
In HCM, avoid dehydration and vasodilators, screen first-degree relatives, and assess sudden death risk.
In DCM, treat heart failure and arrhythmia, stop alcohol and cardiotoxins, and consider genetic counselling.

blocks.title: Do not give antibiotics before cultures if the patient is stable
blocks.text: Starting antibiotics before blood cultures can render them negative, removing the organism and sensitivities needed to choose therapy. The exception is a critically unwell patient, in whom treatment must not be delayed once cultures are taken.

points: Infective endocarditis arises when bacteraemia seeds a thrombus on damaged endothelium; diagnosis uses the modified Duke criteria, and three separate blood-culture sets before antibiotics are the key investigation.
Echocardiography (transthoracic then transoesophageal) identifies vegetations, abscesses and valve damage.
Cardiomyopathies are dilated, hypertrophic, restrictive or arrhythmogenic; each has a distinct structure, presentation and examination clue.
UK guidance does not recommend routine antibiotic prophylaxis; some guidelines restrict it to the highest-risk patients and procedures, and good oral hygiene is emphasised.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a major criterion in the modified Duke criteria?

options.text: Viridans streptococci grown from two separate blood-culture sets

questions.correctOptionText: Viridans streptococci grown from two separate blood-culture sets

distractorRationale.b: Correct: a typical organism in two separate sets is a major microbiological criterion.
distractorRationale.c: A predisposing factor is a minor criterion.
distractorRationale.d: Osler nodes are an immunological minor criterion.

questions.explanation: The major criteria are positive blood cultures for typical organisms and evidence of endocardial involvement on imaging. Fever, predisposition and vascular or immunological phenomena are minor criteria.

questions.stem: A haemodynamically stable 55-year-old woman with a known mitral valve prolapse has had 10 days of fever and a new murmur. Which blood culture strategy is best?

options.text: One set from a peripheral vein after starting empirical antibiotics
At least three sets from separate venepuncture sites before any antibiotic, spaced over at least an hour
A single set from a central line
No cultures, treat on clinical grounds

questions.correctOptionText: At least three sets from separate venepuncture sites before any antibiotic, spaced over at least an hour

distractorRationale.a: Starting antibiotics first and sending a single set risks negative cultures.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: multiple separate sets before antibiotics maximise yield and show continuous bacteraemia.
distractorRationale.c: A single set from a line risks contamination and low yield.
distractorRationale.d: The organism and sensitivities are required to choose therapy.

questions.explanation: Endocarditis causes a continuous low-grade bacteraemia, so several independent sets taken before antibiotics give the best yield and help distinguish true infection from skin contamination. A stable patient allows time for spacing.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old woman with rheumatic mitral stenosis has a temperature of 38.6 degrees Celsius and a splenic infarct on CT. Two separate blood-culture sets grow viridans streptococci. Using the modified Duke criteria, how many criteria does he meet and what is the classification?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: viridans streptococci in two sets is major; valve disease, fever and a splenic infarct (vascular phenomenon) are three minor criteria.
distractorRationale.b: 1 major plus 1 minor is only possible endocarditis, and he meets more.
distractorRationale.c: The positive typical-organism cultures are a major criterion.
distractorRationale.d: He meets more than 2 minor criteria and one major.

questions.explanation: Viridans streptococci in two separate sets is a major criterion. Predisposition (rheumatic valve disease), fever above 38.0 degrees Celsius and a vascular phenomenon (splenic infarct) give three minor criteria, and 1 major plus 3 minor is definite endocarditis.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old footballer collapses during a match. His father died suddenly at 40. Examination reveals an ejection systolic murmur that gets louder when he stands from a squat. Which condition is most likely?

distractorRationale.a: DCM presents with heart failure and a dilated LV rather than sudden collapse with this murmur.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: young, family history of sudden death, exertional collapse and a murmur increased by reducing preload suggest HCM.
distractorRationale.c: Restrictive disease causes right heart failure and is rare in young athletes.
distractorRationale.d: No fever or infective features are given.

questions.explanation: Standing or Valsalva reduces venous return and LV volume, narrowing the outflow tract and increasing the murmur; squatting does the opposite. Autosomal dominant inheritance and sudden cardiac death in young athletes are classic for HCM.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man has progressive ankle swelling, a raised JVP that rises on inspiration, a low-voltage ECG and echocardiography showing thickened ventricular walls with a normal ejection fraction. Which cardiomyopathy is most likely?

distractorRationale.a: DCM has a dilated, poorly contracting ventricle, not thick walls with preserved EF.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: stiff thick walls with preserved EF, Kussmaul sign and low voltage point to infiltrative restrictive disease such as amyloid.
distractorRationale.c: Takotsubo follows acute stress with apical ballooning.
distractorRationale.d: Alcoholic disease is dilated with reduced EF.

questions.explanation: Infiltration of the myocardium with amyloid thickens and stiffens the walls, impairing filling, while the low voltage on ECG despite thick walls is a clue. A rise in venous pressure on inspiration (Kussmaul sign) reflects impaired right ventricular filling.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old with a mechanical aortic valve is booked for a dental extraction. Under current UK guidance, what is the recommendation about antibiotic prophylaxis against endocarditis?

options.text: Routine prophylaxis is not recommended; emphasise oral hygiene and prompt treatment of any dental infection
Prophylaxis is mandatory for every dental procedure
Prophylaxis is only for patients with hypertension
Prophylaxis is replaced by lifelong aspirin

questions.correctOptionText: Routine prophylaxis is not recommended; emphasise oral hygiene and prompt treatment of any dental infection

distractorRationale.a: Correct: UK guidance advises against routine antibiotic prophylaxis, even in higher-risk patients, while stressing oral hygiene.
distractorRationale.b: UK guidance does not recommend routine prophylaxis.

questions.explanation: Prophylaxis prevents few cases because routine daily bacteraemia from chewing and brushing is more important, and antibiotics carry adverse-effect risk. Some international guidelines restrict it to the highest-risk patients, but UK guidance does not recommend it routinely.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman with heart failure symptoms has echocardiographic end-diastolic volume 200 mL and end-systolic volume 150 mL. Calculate her left ventricular ejection fraction as a percentage.
questions.explanation: Stroke volume = 200 - 150 = 50 mL. LVEF = 50 / 200 x 100 = 25%, which is severely reduced and consistent with dilated cardiomyopathy.

questions.stem: In a 25-year-old man with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, continuous-wave Doppler across the left ventricular outflow tract shows a peak velocity of 3.5 m/s. Using the simplified Bernoulli equation, calculate the peak pressure gradient in mmHg.
questions.explanation: The simplified Bernoulli equation is gradient = 4 x v squared = 4 x 3.5 squared = 4 x 12.25 = 49 mmHg. This is above 30 mmHg, indicating significant outflow tract obstruction.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man with a bicuspid aortic valve presents with 4 weeks of low-grade fevers and weight loss. Explain how you would investigate for infective endocarditis, including the blood culture strategy, imaging and how the modified Duke criteria are applied.
markingGuide: At least three blood-culture sets from separate venepuncture sites, before antibiotics, spaced over at least an hour if stable
Transthoracic echocardiography first, transoesophageal if negative or if prosthetic valve or suspected abscess
Major criteria: typical organism in cultures; endocardial involvement on imaging
Minor criteria: predisposition (bicuspid valve), fever 38 degrees Celsius or above, vascular phenomena, immunological phenomena, non-major positive microbiology
Definite: 2 major, or 1 major plus 3 minor, or 5 minor
Other tests: inflammatory markers, urinalysis for haematuria, ECG for PR prolongation
questions.explanation: Diagnosis requires both microbiological and structural evidence because no single sign is specific. Blood cultures before antibiotics identify the organism, while echocardiography shows valve involvement and complications.

questions.stem: Explain the principles behind antibiotic prophylaxis for infective endocarditis and why current UK guidance limits its use. State who might still be considered for prophylaxis under more restrictive international guidelines.
markingGuide: Transient bacteraemia from procedures was thought to seed damaged valves
Everyday activities (chewing, brushing) cause far more cumulative bacteraemia than single procedures
Prophylaxis prevents very few cases and carries risks (anaphylaxis, resistance, C. difficile)
UK guidance does not recommend routine prophylaxis; emphasise oral hygiene, dental review, early treatment of infections
More restrictive international guidelines limit prophylaxis to highest-risk patients: prosthetic valves, previous endocarditis, certain congenital heart disease, for high-risk dental procedures
Patient education about symptoms and early review for unexplained fever
questions.explanation: Evidence suggests that most endocarditis is not preceded by a dental procedure, so prophylaxis offers little absolute benefit while exposing patients to avoidable antibiotic harm. Restricting any prophylaxis to patients with the worst outcomes concentrates the benefit.
